blocks.text: The opening portrays nations, peoples, kings, and rulers acting together in revolt against the LORD and his anointed one. Their wish to break bonds and throw off cords presents the LORD’s rule and the king’s rule as a yoke they reject.

sections.title: Revolt against the LORD and his anointed

blocks.text: The poem answers the rulers’ coalition by depicting the LORD as enthroned and by announcing that he has installed his king on Zion. The king then reports a decree: he is called God’s “son,” receives the nations as an inheritance, and is given authority symbolized by an iron rod and shattered pottery. This language belongs to a royal idiom, but the psalm itself does not identify one particular accession ceremony or establish borrowing from a specific source. Its closing address turns the conflict into a warning for kings and judges to serve the LORD with fear and rejoicing marked by trembling; the wording of the final expression is disputed in translation.

Psalm 2 is often read with Psalm 1 as an untitled gateway to the collection. Together they place Torah-shaped flourishing and the way of the wicked alongside rebellious nations, the LORD’s kingship, and his anointed king.
